title: Hernia
description: Abnormal exit of tissues or organs from the cavity they usually reside in
wiki_lead:
A hernia (pl.: hernias or herniae, from Latin, meaning 'rupture') is the abnormal exit of tissue or an organ, such as the bowel, through the wall of the cavity in which it normally resides. The term is also used for the normal development of the intestinal tract, referring to the retraction of the intestine from the extra-embryonal navel coelom into the abdomen in the healthy embryo at about 71⁄2 weeks.
Various types of hernias can occur, most commonly involving the abdomen, and specifically the groin. Groin hernias are most commonly inguinal hernias but may also be femoral hernias. Other types of hernias include hiatus, incisional, and umbilical hernias. Symptoms are present in about 66% of people with groin hernias. This may include pain or discomfort in the lower abdomen, especially with coughing, exercise, or urinating or defecating. Often, it gets worse throughout the day and improves when lying down. A bulge may appear at the site of hernia, that becomes larger when bending down.
Groin hernias occur more often on the right than left side. The main concern is bowel strangulation, where the blood supply to part of the bowel is blocked. This usually produces severe pain and tenderness in the area. Hiatus, or hiatal hernias often result in heartburn but may also cause chest pain or pain while eating.
Risk factors for the development of a hernia include smoking, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, obesity, pregnancy, peritoneal dialysis, collagen vascular disease, and previous open appendectomy, among others. Predisposition to hernias is genetic and occur more often in certain families. Deleterious mutations causing predisposition to hernias seem to have dominant inheritance (especially for men). It is unclear if groin hernias are associated with heavy lifting. Hernias can often be diagnosed based on signs and symptoms. Occasionally, medical imaging is used to confirm the diagnosis or rule out other possible causes. The diagnosis of hiatus hernias is often done by endoscopy.
Groin hernias that do not cause symptoms in males do not need immediate surgical repair, a practice referred to as "watchful waiting". However most men tend to eventually undergo groin hernia surgery due to the development of pain. For women, however, repair is generally recommended due to the higher rate of femoral hernias, which have more complications. If strangulation occurs, immediate surgery is required. Repair may be done by open surgery, laparoscopic surgery, or robotic-assisted surgery. Open surgery has the benefit of possibly being done under local anesthesia rather than general anesthesia. Laparoscopic surgery generally has less pain following the procedure. A hiatus hernia may be treated with lifestyle changes such as raising the head of the bed, weight loss and adjusting eating habits. The medications H2 blockers or proton pump inhibitors may help. If the symptoms do not improve with medications, a surgery known as laparoscopic Nissen fundoplication may be an option.
Globally in 2019, there were 32.53 million prevalent cases of inguinal, femoral, and abdominal hernias, with a 95% uncertainty interval ranging from 27.71 to 37.79 million. Additionally, there were 13.02 million incident cases, with an uncertainty interval of 10.68 to 15.49 million. These figures reflect a 36.00% increase in prevalent cases and a 63.67% increase in incident cases compared to the numbers reported in 1990. About 27% of males and 3% of females develop a groin hernia at some point in their lives. Inguinal, femoral and abdominal hernias were present in 18.5 million people and resulted in 59,800 deaths in 2015. Groin hernias occur most often before the age of 1 and after the age of 50. It is not known how commonly hiatus hernias occur, with estimates in North America varying from 10% to 80%. The first known description of a hernia dates back to at least 1550 BC, in the Ebers Papyrus from Egypt.

grok_lead: A hernia is a medical condition in which an organ or other tissue protrudes through a weak spot or opening in the surrounding muscle or connective tissue, most commonly in the abdominal wall, forming a visible bulge that may cause discomfort or pain. This protrusion often involves the intestines or fatty tissue pushing through the peritoneum, the lining of the abdominal cavity, into adjacent areas like the groin or thigh. Hernias can be present at birth or develop later due to factors such as increased abdominal pressure, and while many are reducibleâmeaning the bulge can be pushed backâthey carry risks of complications if untreated. Hernias are categorized by their location and underlying causes, with inguinal hernias being the most prevalent, accounting for about 75% of cases and primarily affecting men as intestinal tissue bulges into the inguinal canal in the groin area. Other common types include hiatal hernias, where the upper stomach pushes through the diaphragm into the chest cavity and affects around 20% of U.S. adults, often leading to gastroesophageal reflux; umbilical hernias, which occur near the belly button and are frequent in infants or during pregnancy; and incisional hernias, which develop at sites of prior abdominal surgery due to weakened scar tissue. Less common variants, such as femoral or epigastric hernias, arise in the upper thigh or between the breastbone and navel, respectively, and may require prompt intervention to prevent progression. The development of a hernia typically stems from a combination of congenital weaknesses in the abdominal wall and acquired factors that increase intra-abdominal pressure, including chronic coughing, constipation, obesity, heavy lifting, pregnancy, or previous surgical incisions. Risk factors are more pronounced in certain demographics: men face higher rates of inguinal hernias (affecting nearly 25% over a lifetime), while women are prone to femoral and umbilical types, and older adults or those with connective tissue disorders like cystic fibrosis may experience earlier onset. Symptoms often include a noticeable lump that may disappear when lying down, along with aching pressure, sharp pain during straining, or, in hiatal cases, heartburn and regurgitation; severe indicators like sudden intense pain, nausea, vomiting, fever, inability to pass stool or gas, or a discolored bulge signal a strangulated hernia, a medical emergency where blood supply to the trapped tissue is cut off. Diagnosis generally involves a physical examination, where a healthcare provider assesses the bulge during activities like cough ing or standing, supplemented by imaging such as ultrasound or CT scans if the hernia is not easily reducible or internal complications are suspected. Treatment is primarily surgical, with options ranging from open repair using stitches or synthetic mesh to minimally invasive laparoscopic or robotic techniques that reduce recovery time and recurrence rates; watchful waiting may apply to small, asymptomatic hernias, while hiatal hernias might be managed with medications for reflux alongside procedures like Nissen fundoplication. Prevention strategies emphasize maintaining a healthy weight, using proper lifting techniques, treating chronic conditions like constipation or cough, and avoiding excessive straining to minimize abdominal pressure.
